evaluated.name: Gambling For Resurrection Intensity
evaluated.hypothesis: Reinvestment relative to the installed capital base is value-destroying in proportion to how deep a firm's accumulated earnings deficit is, because equity holders of firms with large historical losses have convex payoffs and prefer risky expansion over debt repayment.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the hard INDICATOR with a winsorized, standardized retained-earnings-to-assets conditioner removes the degenerate zero mass and the reliance on a small negative-book-equity subsample: every firm now receives a continuous score and coverage matches capx and re availability. Centering at zero makes the interaction genuinely two-sided, so heavy investors with deep accumulated profits form the long leg and heavy investors with accumulated deficits form the short leg, while low-investment firms of either type sit near zero and do not drive the spread.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Financing Gap Amplified By Thin Working Capital
evaluated.hypothesis: An investment program that exceeds internally generated cash flow is only dangerous when the firm has no working-capital slack to bridge it; the same gap at a firm with ample net working capital is a normal, self-correcting funding cycle rather than a solvency event.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the additive SUMRANK the critic identified as inconsistent with the stated mechanism: the funding-gap rank is non-negative and is multiplied by a centered working-capital z-score, so firms with no gap score near zero regardless of their balance sheet and the spread is identified purely off how the gap is cushioned. That construction breaks the standalone net-external-financing and cash-holdings effects, since a large gap can now appear on either the long or the short side depending on the slack available to absorb it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unsold Capacity Build Under Solvency Strain
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment that shows up as unsold inventory rather than revenue is evidence that demand has not validated the expansion, and such unvalidated working-capital investment is followed by fire-sale markdowns precisely in firms whose current assets barely cover their obligations.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the rank-difference of asset growth and profitability that FF5 spans through CMA and RMW; the investment channel is now a change in inventory days (a real-quantity, demand-validation measure that is not an asset-growth or ROA proxy) and the distress channel is the Altman-style working-capital-to-liabilities cushion in centered form. The multiplicative structure means firms with stable inventory turns score near zero whatever their solvency, so the long-short spread is driven by the joint event of inventory accumulation plus a thin solvency buffer rather than by either well-known factor.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Conjunctive Self-Funded Resilience
evaluated.hypothesis: Financial resilience requires investment to be simultaneously self-funded and backstopped by liquid reserves; a firm scores high only if its operating cash flow covers its capital spending and its cash covers near-term obligations, and such firms are undervalued relative to their low refinancing risk.
evaluated.reasoning: MIN of the two ranks enforces the logical AND that the critic correctly noted SUMRANK does not deliver: a cash-rich firm that outspends its cash flow, or a self-funding firm with no liquidity, is capped at the low leg, so neither channel alone can produce a high score. It is also not merely the inverse of low investment, because a capital-intensive firm whose operating cash flow exceeds its capex still ranks highly, which separates the signal from CMA and from the short-side proposals in this set.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Conjunctive Distressed Overinvestment
evaluated.hypothesis: Reinvestment intensity relative to the installed capital base destroys equity value specifically at firms carrying high net debt, where new assets collateralize existing creditors and expansion is a levered bet rather than value creation.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the deliberate short-side mirror of the archive's winning conjunctive structure: the MIN of two ranks is high only when a firm is simultaneously a heavy reinvestor and net-debt-laden, so neither the asset-growth anomaly nor the leverage effect alone can drive the extreme decile. Netting cash out of total liabilities separates true balance-sheet strain from firms that gross up both sides, which is what makes it more than a CMA re-weighting.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Forced Contraction Under Illiquidity
evaluated.hypothesis: For fragile firms the danger is not only overexpansion but forced contraction: shrinking the productive capital base while working capital is thin relative to total liabilities indicates asset sales made under creditor pressure at distressed prices, which predicts further equity value destruction.
evaluated.reasoning: This deliberately probes the opposite corner of the investment-distress plane from every other proposal, testing whether the interaction is monotone in investment or U-shaped — an answer that reshapes the entire search direction regardless of outcome. If both this and the overinvestment conjunction earn negative alphas, the correct future construction is a distress-conditioned distance-from-normal-investment measure rather than a signed investment level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Chronic Funding Gap With Short-Debt Reliance
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of investment above earnings is a normal lumpy-capex event, but a persistent three-year gap funded at the short end of the maturity curve is a structural dependence on rollover markets that is punished when credit conditions turn.
evaluated.reasoning: The new element is persistence — the three-year moving average removes lumpy one-off capex from the investment leg — combined with a rollover-risk conditioner (short-term debt relative to cash) that is distinct from leverage level and therefore not spanned by CMA or by the other proposals here. If the persistent version dominates the one-year gap signal from generation 0, chronic external dependence rather than transient financing need is the priced state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Self-Funded Expansion Without Leverage
evaluated.hypothesis: The rare firms that step up capital renewal while simultaneously reducing their liability ratio are demonstrating that expansion is being paid for out of internally generated cash; this revealed funding capacity is a forward-looking resilience signal that neither the investment level nor the leverage level discloses.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the archive winner's structure entirely rather than substituting one input: both legs are now first differences, so the signal is orthogonal to the profitability level and to the asset-growth level that the critic identified inside (ib − capx)/at. Because rising capex normally coincides with rising leverage, the conjunction isolates a genuinely small and economically meaningful corner — accelerating investment funded without new claims — and the MIN guarantees that deleveraging alone (a distress-recovery signal) cannot carry the long leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Added Without Utilization
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment is validated by throughput, not by spending: when a firm's sales per unit of installed fixed capital deteriorates, the capital base has grown ahead of demand, and this overhang becomes an equity value problem specifically for firms whose expansion is locked in by long-term debt that cannot be scaled back with utilization.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the acquisition channel — which the critic correctly flagged as the published post-merger drift anomaly plus a degenerate COALESCE tie mass — with a capacity-utilization channel that has no tied values and full coverage from sale, ppent, dltt and at. Falling fixed-asset turnover is a change in productive efficiency rather than an investment or profitability level, so it is not spanned by CMA or RMW, and the long-term-debt conditioner captures the irreversibility that turns idle capacity into distress.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Runway Depletion Funding Capex
evaluated.hypothesis: What predicts distress is not the level of cash but its trajectory relative to near-term obligations: a firm spending heavily on fixed assets while its cash-to-current-liabilities coverage is actively eroding is consuming its own runway, and each additional quarter of that trajectory raises the probability of a forced financing event.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops sstk and therefore drops any overlap with the net-share-issuance and external-financing anomalies the critic named, replacing them with a liquidity-trajectory channel built from a first difference in coverage, which is not a documented standalone factor. The conjunction is essential and asymmetric: heavy investors whose coverage is stable or improving score low, and firms depleting cash without investing (ordinary operating losses) also score low, so only the self-inflicted runway burn survives into the short leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Headcount Expansion Without Earnings Cover
evaluated.hypothesis: Labor is the least reversible and most cash-hungry form of investment, so headcount expansion by firms whose earnings barely cover their obligations commits the firm to a fixed cost structure it cannot service, and the subsequent restructuring is not anticipated by investors focused on capital spending.
evaluated.reasoning: Employment growth is a real-quantity investment measure that appears in no FF5 factor and in no archive signal, and unlike capex it cannot be funded by depreciation or reversed by simply pausing a project. Conditioning on earnings-to-total-liabilities rather than on leverage keeps the fragility leg tied to debt-service capacity, so the top corner is specifically firms hiring into a coverage problem.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Erratic Capital Budgeting Under Accumulated Deficit
evaluated.hypothesis: The instability of an investment program, not its level, reveals whether capital allocation is planned or opportunistic; firms whose capex intensity swings wildly while they carry an accumulated earnings deficit are allocating capital reactively to funding availability, and such firms face higher realized distress costs.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests a second-moment investment concept that no factor model and no archive signal spans — every prior proposal used levels, changes, or persistence of investment, never its volatility — and pairs it with retained earnings, the Altman input that measures cumulative rather than current fragility. If instability carries information beyond the level, it justifies a whole family of second-moment conditioners for later generations; if not, we can drop the dimension cheaply.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Validated Versus Unvalidated Expansion
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(sale, at), 1)), RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1))), MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(sale, at), 1))), RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Expansion is priced correctly only when the market can see whether it is being absorbed by demand: capacity growth accompanied by rising asset turnover is validated investment and should earn a premium, while identical capacity growth accompanied by falling turnover is unabsorbed capacity heading for write-downs.
evaluated.reasoning: This keeps the two-sided repair for the null-FMB problem but abandons the net-debt and cash-coverage constructs the critic identified, so the spread cannot collapse into a leverage-liquidity tilt: both corners share the same investment leg and differ only in the sign of the turnover change, making the signal a pure sign-flipping conditional that is near zero for non-investors. It therefore cannot be reproduced by CMA, which sorts on the level of growth without regard to whether output followed, and it uses only high-coverage annual items rather than the oancf-restricted sample.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Intangible Expansion Against Tangible Collateral
evaluated.hypothesis: Creditors lend against liquidation value, so a firm shifting the composition of its asset base toward intangibles while its liabilities already tower over its tangible capital is eroding the collateral backing its debt, raising both the probability and the deadweight cost of default.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the accrual-versus-cash ablation with an untouched economic axis — the composition rather than the level of investment — where the fragility conditioner is liabilities per unit of pledgeable tangible capital rather than any profitability or cash measure, so it is not a q-theory or RMW-CMA restatement. The conjunction matters because intangible-heavy expansion is benign at firms with light liabilities and heavy liabilities are survivable when backed by hard assets; only the joint state destroys recovery value.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Growth Financed By Current Liabilities
evaluated.hypothesis: Funding long-lived, irreversible plant with an expanding stock of current liabilities — trade credit, accruals, and short-dated bank lines — creates a maturity mismatch that must be rolled continuously, so the same capacity build is far more fragile when the financing appears at the short end of the balance sheet.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the tax framing the critic reduced to investment-times-low-profitability and replaces it with a financing-structure mechanism containing no profitability leg at all, so it cannot be a noisy RMW proxy. It also repairs the generation-0 proposal that the validator rejected for lacking a distress-exclusive variable, and it is distinguishable from the archived short-debt signal because it conditions on the *change* in current-liability intensity rather than on a static cash-coverage ratio.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Resources Versus Committed Uses
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is a coverage ratio: total available internal resources — this year's operating cash flow plus the cash stock — measured against the claims that must be met in cash over the next year, namely the capital spending program plus maturing short-term debt.
evaluated.reasoning: This expresses the winning mechanism as a single smooth coverage ratio rather than a conjunction of two ranks, which makes it monotone over the entire cross-section and should produce an FMB slope and a decile spread that finally measure the same object. It is a genuine investment-distress interaction because the investment program sits in the denominator alongside maturing debt — capex is treated as a mandatory claim on cash, which is precisely the economics of the theme — and it is not a coverage ratio published as a standalone anomaly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Persistent Expansion Despite Chronic Losses
evaluated.hypothesis: Current-year losses are noisy, but the frequency of loss years over five years identifies firms with a structurally unviable business model; when such firms sustain three consecutive years of heavy capital spending relative to their installed base, they are compounding a failing franchise with irreversible outlays.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archived fragility conditioner has been a current-period balance-sheet or income ratio, whereas loss *frequency* is the chronicity measure that the distress-prediction literature finds dominates single-period ratios, and pairing it with cumulative rather than one-year investment tests whether persistence on both sides sharpens the interaction. The tied values in the loss-frequency leg are economically meaningful buckets rather than a degenerate zero mass, and the MIN ensures profitable serial investors and chronically unprofitable non-investors both stay out of the short leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Funded Versus Unfunded Investment Ramp
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(che, lct))), MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: An acceleration in capital spending is good news when the firm already holds the liquidity to pay for it and bad news when it does not, so the *same* investment ramp should predict opposite returns depending on the liquidity state — the core claim of the investment-distress theme stated as a sign flip rather than as a level effect.
evaluated.reasoning: Both terms share an identical investment leg and differ only in the direction of the liquidity conditioner, so the signal is mechanically zero for firms not changing their investment rate and cannot reduce to either a standalone investment sort or a standalone cash-holdings sort — it measures only the interaction. It uses no cash-flow-statement item, so it tests the funded-versus-unfunded story on roughly 60% more firm-months than the archive winner, telling us whether the oancf coverage cost is worth paying.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Smooth Funding Capacity Product
evaluated.hypothesis: Funding capacity for the investment program has two multiplicatively interacting dimensions — how many times over this year's operating cash flow covers this year's capital spending, and how much of the near-term obligation stack the cash stock can retire — and firms strong on both are the resilient investors the theme predicts.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic's algebra is correct that any symmetric difference of a conjunction and its complement collapses to the additive rank sum, so instead of a two-sided construction I change the operator geometry: the rank product is strictly increasing in both legs everywhere, whereas MIN has zero gradient in whichever leg is currently larger, which is the most plausible reason the archive's MIN slopes were flat while its decile spreads were significant. The self-funding leg is also re-specified as a scale-free coverage multiple rather than an asset-scaled difference, removing the size confound that a /at scaling introduces.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Rollover Pressure On An Illiquid Asset Base
evaluated.hypothesis: Maturity mismatch bites when maturing *debt* — not trade payables — must be repaid by a firm whose assets are locked into fixed plant: such a firm cannot liquidate to meet the claim and must refinance on whatever terms creditors offer, so equity bears the full rollover risk.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the mis-specified conditioner the critic identified: lct/lt rewarded payables-only firms with a score of 1.0, whereas dlc/act is zero for firms with no short-term borrowing and rises only when maturing debt is large relative to the assets that could actually be converted to cash. The interaction is essential and untested in the archive — high tangibility is benign without maturing debt, and short-term debt is manageable when the balance sheet is liquid — and both legs are bounded ratios with full sample coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Irreversible Capex Against Volatile Earnings
evaluated.hypothesis: Default risk rises with the volatility of the earnings stream that must service fixed commitments, so committing to irreversible capital outlays is far more dangerous for firms whose return on assets swings widely; the market prices the level of profitability but underprices the interaction between its instability and investment irreversibility.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the industry-ranking knob — which the critic rightly judged uninformative given that the flat slopes are an operator artifact — with the canonical second-moment distress input from the bankruptcy-prediction literature, a dimension the archive has never used on the fragility side. The rank product keeps the mapping monotone in both legs, and pairing earnings volatility with irreversible investment is economically distinct from the failed capex-volatility signal, which measured instability of the investment policy itself rather than of the cash flows that must fund it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Post-Investment Obligation Surplus
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically decisive quantity is the cash surplus that remains after a firm funds its investment program and retires its maturing debt, measured against the total obligation stack it must eventually service; firms with a positive surplus relative to liabilities can absorb shocks without external capital, and this capacity is underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: Expressing coverage as a difference rather than a quotient removes the two defects the critic identified in the archive's best-alpha signal — a denominator that approaches zero for firms with no capex and no short debt, and a numerator that can flip sign — so the ordering no longer pools opposite states; scaling by total liabilities makes the distress side the metric of the surplus, which is what turns a free-cash-flow measure into a genuine investment-distress interaction. If this recovers the +7% alpha while lifting the FMB slope, the family is consolidated in a single monotone variable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Flow-Only Coverage Of Committed Uses
evaluated.hypothesis: Recurring operating cash flow, not the accumulated cash pile, is what determines whether a firm can fund its capital program and roll its maturing debt without capital-market access; if so, coverage measured from the flow alone should carry the abnormal return and the cash stock is incidental.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the decisive diagnostic for the leading family, because every member so far mixes a stock leg (che) with a flow leg, leaving open the possibility that the alpha is the documented cash-holdings effect wearing an investment costume. Dropping the stock entirely gives a clean answer: if the alpha survives, the mechanism is genuinely investment-funding capacity and future refinements should build on flows; if it collapses, the archive's results are a liquidity-level premium and the search must be redirected.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustainable Earnings Coverage Of Commitments
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm's ability to fund investment and debt internally depends on its *sustainable* earning power rather than one year's realization, so a three-year average of income before extraordinary items plus the cash stock, netted against committed uses and scaled by obligations, should capture the same resilience state as the cash-flow version.
evaluated.reasoning: Every leading signal is confined to the post-SFAS-95 cash-flow sample (coverage 0.078–0.089 against an attainable 0.135), so the binding constraint on statistical reliability is now data availability rather than mechanism; smoothing income over three years addresses the reason a single year's accrual earnings is a poor proxy for funding capacity, namely transitory items and accrual noise. A comparable alpha at materially higher coverage would let the remaining generations work with roughly 50% more firm-months, and a weaker result would establish that cash realization — not earning power — is the priced ingredient.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Expansion Into Revenue Decline
evaluated.hypothesis: Reinvesting heavily in the installed capital base while revenue is actually contracting is the clearest case of value-destroying expansion: the firm is adding capacity to a shrinking business, so the outlay is a sunk claim on future cash rather than a growth option.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's utilization signal used a turnover *change* paired with long-term debt and produced α −4.6% with a null slope under MIN; here the fragility conditioner is an outright sales decline — the most visible and most persistent distress state — and the rank product keeps the mapping strictly monotone in both legs, which is the construction that lifted FMB slopes elsewhere. Both inputs are high-coverage annual items, giving the short side of the theme a candidate that does not depend on the cash-flow statement.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Successful Versus Failed Retrenchment
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(che, lct), 1))), MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lct), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital-spending cuts are ambiguous news until you observe where the freed cash went: retrenchment that visibly rebuilds cash coverage of near-term obligations is a successful repair, whereas an identical cut accompanied by continued erosion of coverage means the cut was too late to matter and the firm is still losing ground.
evaluated.reasoning: The revision removes the second same-signed anomaly leg the critic objected to — falling debt is replaced by the *direction of the liquidity response*, which is not a documented standalone effect — so neither leg predicts returns on its own and the signal is mechanically near zero for firms that do not change their investment rate. It applies the two-sided conditional geometry that produced the archive's highest reliability (ls_talpha 4.93) to the contraction side of the theme, where the archive currently has only an unconditional forced-contraction result (α −3.8%) and therefore cannot distinguish repair from decline.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Coverage Premium Conditioned On Obligation Load
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(oancf, ADD(capx, dlc))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, ADD(capx, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Internal coverage of the capital program and maturing debt should be priced most strongly where the obligation load is heaviest, because that is where the marginal consequence of a funding shortfall is default rather than a postponed project; among firms with negligible liabilities the same coverage carries little information.
evaluated.reasoning: This construction eliminates the leverage main effect the critic identified: at median coverage the two MIN terms are identical for every leverage value, so the signal is exactly zero and cannot load on leverage per se, while the coverage ranking is amplified as the liability rank rises. It therefore tests the interaction claim itself rather than a leverage tilt, and unlike a ZSCORE-centered product it stays bounded and monotone in coverage, the property that has consistently separated signals with real FMB slopes from those with null slopes in this archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Conjunctive Coverage Of Investment And Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Resilience requires both a sustainable earnings surplus after investment relative to total obligations and a cash stock large enough to cover near-term claims *including* the coming year's capital program; firms strong on both dimensions are those for which no shock forces external financing.
evaluated.reasoning: This settles the operator question at full coverage: the additive smooth ratios produce alphas with weak slopes while rank conjunctions reorder firms in a way that has repeatedly lifted FMB t-stats above 3.5, and here both legs come from the highest-coverage inputs so the test is not confounded by sample size. Adding capx to the denominator of the liquidity leg is also a substantive improvement over the archived che/lct, since it makes the liquidity requirement depend on the firm's own investment commitment rather than on obligations alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earnings Coverage Where Investment Is Largest
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(ib, lt)), RANK(RATIO(capx, at))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ib, lt))), RANK(RATIO(capx, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The theme's core claim is conditional: earnings coverage of obligations should matter most for firms with large capital programs, because that is where a shortfall must be met by creditors or by abandoning committed projects, and least for firms that are barely investing.
evaluated.reasoning: The construction is exactly zero at median coverage for every level of investment, so it cannot load on the investment main effect, and it is zero for low-investment firms, so it cannot load on the profitability main effect either — it measures only the interaction, which is what the theme asks for and what the earlier uncentered rank product failed to isolate. It uses only high-coverage items, and the analogous leverage-conditioned version already produced fmb 2.38, so the design is known to generate cross-sectional information.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Coverage Gap Amplified By Short Maturity Reliance
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ib, DELTA(wcap, 1)), capx), lt))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A funding shortfall becomes a distress event only when the claims come due soon: firms whose cash earnings fail to cover their capital program are vulnerable in proportion to how much of their debt sits at the short end of the maturity structure and therefore must be renegotiated immediately.
evaluated.reasoning: This gives the short side the same economic content as the family's successful long side while conditioning on maturity structure rather than on leverage level, so the timing of refinancing — not the amount of debt — supplies the amplification, an axis the archive has never tested. Both legs are monotone ranks computed from full-coverage inputs, and the shortfall leg is the exact mirror of Signal 1, which lets us verify whether the family's information is symmetric across tails or concentrated on the resilient side as the MIN-based results suggest.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquid Resources Against The Investment Program
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm's net liquid resources should be judged against the size of the capital program it is actually running plus the debt it must retire: net working capital that covers three years of capital spending and maturing short-term debt means the program can be completed without creditors, while a fraction of one year's spending means every project is hostage to refinancing.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the depreciation-omitting cash proxy entirely, so the signal contains no accrual and no earnings component and cannot be a blend of the Sloan and profitability anomalies; it is built only from a liquidity stock and the scale of committed uses. Using cumulative three-year capex as the program size also stabilises the denominator that the critic flagged in the archived ratio, since one-off capex years no longer push firms to the extremes, and coverage is full because no cash-flow-statement item is required.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Funding Capacity At Its Own Historical Low
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, capx), lt)), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, capx), lt), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cross-sectional funding capacity is contaminated by permanent industry differences in capital intensity, so what identifies a firm sliding toward strain is being simultaneously low against peers *and* at the bottom of its own five-year range; conversely, a firm at a personal high in coverage is being re-rated upward, and the market adjusts slowly.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the rejected input substitution with a genuinely new dimension the archive has never used — position within a firm's *own* history of funding capacity, which is immune to the industry-level heterogeneity that makes pooled ranks of capital-intensity ratios hard to interpret. The conjunction of level and own-history position means neither a permanently strong firm nor a temporarily improving weak firm scores at the extremes, so the signal isolates firms whose funding capacity is both absolutely and relatively deteriorating.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Claim Composition Conditioned On Capacity Commitment
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(dlc, lct))), RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1))), MIN(RANK(RATIO(dlc, lct)), RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Committing to irreversible capacity is safe when the near-term claim stack is trade credit that rolls with the business, and dangerous when it is contractual debt that must be repaid on a fixed date; the composition of near-term claims should therefore flip the sign of the capacity-expansion signal rather than predict returns on its own.
evaluated.reasoning: The centered construction removes both main effects the critic identified: at median claim composition the two MIN terms are identical so the expansion effect cancels exactly, and for firms with no capacity growth the signal is zero so the maturity-structure effect cancels exactly, leaving only the interaction. It also abandons the capx/ppent leg that has repeatedly produced weak alphas, using gross PP&E growth instead to capture irreversible commitments, which is the specific quantity that a fixed repayment date makes costly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Broad Coverage Index
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), MA(capx, 3)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx)), RATIO(SUB(act, lct), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), dlc))))
evaluated.hypothesis: If funding capacity is a single latent state observed with noise through several accounting windows, averaging three imperfect coverage measures should estimate it more precisely than requiring a firm to be strong on all of them at once.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's conjunctions and its smooth ratios have never been compared as aggregation rules on an identical set of channels, and the difference matters economically: multiplication says the conditions are complements (a firm fails if any one fails), while averaging says they are substitutes measuring one underlying state. Because averaging populates the extremes with firms that are consistently rather than extremely strong, it should also raise portfolio stability, addressing the modest Sharpe (0.33) of the current leader.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Doubly Strained Investor Corner
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), MA(capx, 3)), lt))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The firms that should be most severely mispriced are those failing both funding tests at once — a sustained earnings deficit after investment relative to obligations combined with a cash stock too small to cover near-term claims and the capital program — because for them any shock converts committed investment into a solvency event.
evaluated.reasoning: This occupies the exact opposite corner of the archive leader using the same two legs, which answers a question no prior test has: whether the coverage family's abnormal return comes from the resilient tail, the strained tail, or both symmetrically. The answer is directly actionable for the final generations — if the strained corner alone delivers a large negative alpha, the concluding signal should be built to concentrate the short leg rather than to span both tails.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expansion At A Funding Capacity Trough
evaluated.hypothesis: Mistimed expansion is the distinctive error of fragile firms: accelerating capital spending precisely when the firm's own ability to service obligations from earnings sits at the bottom of its five-year range reveals that the investment decision is not being disciplined by internal funding conditions.
evaluated.reasoning: The own-history dimension is the only new axis from generation 5 that produced a correctly signed cross-sectional slope (fmb 2.37), and pairing it with the *change* in investment intensity rather than its level tests timing rather than scale — a mechanism distinct from every coverage-level signal in the archive. Because within-firm position is measured relative to each firm's own distribution, it is immune to the industry capital-intensity differences that contaminate pooled ranks of investment ratios.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Surplus After Investment And Maturing Debt
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), ADD(MA(capx, 3), dlc)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, MA(capx, 3)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Committed uses of cash comprise both the capital program and the debt that matures within the year, so the earnings surplus that matters for resilience is what remains after funding investment *and* retiring short-term debt, measured against the total obligation stack.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive member that placed maturing debt alongside capex in committed uses produced the largest alphas (+7.4%, +7.2%), but all were confined to the `oancf` sample, so this tests whether that ingredient survives at full coverage inside the conjunctive structure that supplies the FMB slope. If it does, the family's best version combines the alpha-generating definition of committed uses with the slope-generating operator geometry, which is the natural end point of this line of search.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Coverage Level Times Self-Funding Habit
evaluated.hypothesis: Resilience requires both a currently adequate surplus after investment and a demonstrated habit of funding capital spending internally; a firm that has earned more than it invested in most of the last five years has revealed a business model that does not require capital markets, whereas one good year of surplus at a habitually externally-financed firm is not informative.
evaluated.reasoning: The second leg is a *frequency* statistic — the fraction of the last five years in which earnings exceeded capital spending — which is a genuinely different measurement of the same economic condition than a magnitude, so unlike the rejected version the two legs are not the same variable rescaled and can diverge sharply for lumpy investors and cyclical firms. Loss-frequency conditioning of this type produced the archive's only chronicity evidence, and applying it to funding rather than to profitability keeps the signal inside the investment-distress interaction rather than reducing to a profitability sort.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Funding Surplus Per Unit Of Earnings Risk
evaluated.hypothesis: A given surplus after investment buys very different protection depending on how volatile the earnings stream is: a surplus equal to two percent of obligations is comfortable when return on assets moves by one point a year and worthless when it moves by ten, so the priced quantity is the number of earnings shocks the firm can absorb while still funding its capital program.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the rejected smoothing knob with a distance-to-distress construction — surplus scaled by the standard deviation of the shock that threatens it — which is the structural form used by bankruptcy models and which no archive signal has employed, since earnings volatility previously entered only as a multiplicative conditioner and failed. Scaling rather than multiplying is the economically correct use of a second moment here, and it should sharpen both tails: capital-intensive stable firms rise and volatile marginal investors fall, which is precisely the ordering the coverage family currently gets only partially right.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Realized Cash And Sustainable Earnings Complements
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(oancf, che), ADD(capx, dlc))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: This year's realized cash resources against committed uses and the three-year sustainable earnings surplus against total obligations answer different questions — can the firm pay now, and can it keep paying — and firms that satisfy both are more resilient than either measure alone indicates.
evaluated.reasoning: These are the archive's highest-alpha construct (+7.4%, t 4.48, but fmb 1.24) and its highest-slope construct (fmb 4.41), and they have never been combined; because the first is a current-year cash ratio and the second a multi-year accrual surplus scaled by a different denominator, the product is not a rescaling of either. The cost is the 0.089 `oancf` sample, which makes this the natural counterpart to Signal 1: together they show whether the full-coverage backfill or the restricted-sample combination is the better route to a high alpha with a reliable slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Coverage Level Times Coverage Improvement
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ib, capx), lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A strong funding position that is still improving signals a firm moving away from any need for external capital, whereas the same level in deterioration is a firm on its way into the strained corner; the market extrapolates the level and underreacts to the direction.
evaluated.reasoning: Every coverage signal in the archive is a level or a smoothed level, so the trajectory dimension is untested inside the family that actually works, and it is economically distinct because the change is dominated by the most recent year while the three-year average deliberately suppresses it. Unlike the frequency and volatility enrichments that destroyed alpha by discarding magnitude, this leg preserves a continuous magnitude ordering, which is the property those failures suggest matters.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Triple Channel Coverage Conjunction
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), dlc)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Three complementary conditions — a sustainable earnings surplus after investment, a cash stock covering near-term claims plus the capital program, and net working capital covering the multi-year program plus maturing debt — must all hold for a firm to be immune to financing shocks, and requiring all three concentrates the extreme portfolios on genuinely unconstrained firms.
evaluated.reasoning: The additive version of exactly these three channels earned α 4.2% with fmb 1.64 while the two-channel product earned α 5.0% with fmb 4.41, which implies the aggregation rule matters more than the number of channels; this test separates those two effects by holding the channels fixed and switching averaging for multiplication. Each of the three legs has independently produced an alpha above 4% in this archive, so a null result here would be strong evidence that two conditions already exhaust the information.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Coverage Matters More With Unsellable Assets
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(ppent, at))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt))), RANK(RATIO(ppent, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A funding shortfall is survivable for a firm that can sell inventory or receivables and fatal for one whose assets are specialised plant, so the return to funding capacity should be amplified among asset-heavy firms and muted among asset-light ones.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the one economic amplifier the archive has never tested — the redeployability of the asset side, which determines the *cost* of a shortfall rather than its probability — and the centered double-MIN construction sets the signal to exactly zero at median coverage for every tangibility level and to zero for asset-light firms, so neither the tangibility nor the profitability main effect can drive it. It is deliberately the batch's exploratory slot: a positive result identifies where the coverage premium is concentrated and tells the final generation which population to weight.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Retained Funds Surplus Conjunction
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(re, 1), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The funds genuinely available to carry an investment program are the earnings the firm actually retains after honouring its dividend commitments, so the surplus that matters is the annual increment to retained earnings net of capital spending, measured against total obligations.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the biased cash-flow reconstruction entirely — no depreciation term is needed and no observation is backfilled, so the pooled rank cannot proxy for the missing-statement subsample — and replaces it with a quantity the archive has never used in the coverage family: the change in retained earnings, which is income after the dividend claim that a distressed firm can only cut at a reputational cost. Because dividend-paying and non-paying firms with identical earnings receive different scores, the leg is economically distinct from every ib-based surplus already tested, while retaining full sample coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Runway Against The Capital Program
evaluated.hypothesis: The liquidity question posed by the investment-distress interaction is not whether cash covers the liability stack but how many years of the firm's own capital program the cash stock could fund unaided; a firm holding three years of programme spending in cash can complete its projects through any financing freeze.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than relabelling `dlc` between numerator and denominator, this replaces the solvency-style liquidity leg with a pure runway measure defined solely against the firm's own investment commitment, which is the interaction the theme actually specifies and which is far less collinear with the archived `che/lct` and `che/(lct+capx)` legs than a net-cash variant would be. Using the cumulative three-year program as the yardstick also removes the single-year capex lumpiness that makes one-year runway measures noisy, and both inputs are high-coverage items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Restraint Against Own Investment Norm
evaluated.hypothesis: Aggressive or disciplined investment is only meaningful relative to what a firm normally spends, so a capital budget running below its own five-year norm at a firm with solid earnings coverage reveals deliberate restraint by a management team that could afford to spend, which is the resilience the theme predicts.
evaluated.reasoning: Every investment leg in this archive benchmarks capex against assets, plant, or the cross-section, never against the firm's own history, so within-firm abnormal investment is the one untested measurement of the "aggressive versus disciplined" distinction and it is immune to the industry capital-intensity problem that motivates Signal 1. Pairing it with earnings coverage rather than liquidity keeps the interaction squarely on the discipline-versus-strain axis and separates voluntary restraint from the forced contraction that the archive has already shown earns negative alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Surplus Against Contractual Claims Only
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), ADD(dltt, lct))), RANK(RATIO(che, TS_SUM(capx, 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Total liabilities is the wrong denominator for distress because it bundles deferred taxes, pension and other accounting provisions that never trigger a default; the claims that can force a firm into restructuring are long-term debt and the obligations due within the year, and coverage should be measured against those alone.
evaluated.reasoning: This is an economic re-definition of what a claim *is*, not a benchmark swap: it changes which firms are classified as heavily obligated — capital-intensive firms with large deferred tax balances move up, firms with genuine bank and bond debt move down — and that reclassification is the whole content of the test. Pairing it with the runway leg rather than the claims-based liquidity leg also removes the `lct` term from both sides of the conjunction, so the two legs share no variable and the product is not a near-rescale of any evaluated signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earnings Surplus With Collateral Headroom
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ppent, dltt), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Funding capacity is not only cash on hand: a firm whose tangible plant substantially exceeds its long-term debt holds unpledged collateral it can borrow against, so it can carry an investment program through a cash-flow shortfall in a way that an equally cash-poor firm with fully encumbered assets cannot.
evaluated.reasoning: Every liquidity leg tested so far measures realised liquid resources; unused *debt capacity* is a completely different funding channel and has never appeared in this archive, which makes it the least collinear partner available for the earnings-surplus leg. It also sharpens the theme's economics — the same investment program is safe for a firm with borrowing headroom and dangerous for one whose collateral is already pledged — and it uses only full-coverage balance-sheet items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Substitutable Funding Routes
evaluated.expression: MAX(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm needs only one viable route to fund its capital program — either earnings that exceed it or a cash stock that covers it — so the two conditions are substitutes rather than complements, and a firm strong on either should be classified as resilient.
evaluated.reasoning: This poses the opposite economic claim to the entire conjunctive family rather than swapping one near-equivalent operator for another: MAX and MUL disagree sharply about cash-rich loss-makers and cash-poor high-earners, precisely the populations the theme is about, so the two constructions rank the interesting firms very differently. The answer is directly actionable for the final generation — if substitutability wins, the concluding signal should reward either funding route; if it loses, the complements interpretation is confirmed by a test that could have overturned it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Investment Ramp Judged By Earning Power
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt))), MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: An acceleration in capital spending is good news when the firm's sustained earnings already exceed its investment needs and bad news when they do not, so earning power rather than the cash balance is what determines whether an investment ramp should be believed.
evaluated.reasoning: The archived version of this conditional structure earned the highest ls_talpha in the archive (4.93) but the critic correctly noted that among high-ramp firms it collapses to a cash-holdings sort; replacing the conditioner with sustained earnings surplus tests whether the ramp is priced against liquid resources or against the ability to generate them, which is a genuine economic question rather than a parameter choice. The centered construction still removes both main effects, so a positive result cannot be attributed to the investment-change anomaly or to profitability alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Total Resources With Second Line Liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(MA(ib, 3), che), ADD(capx, dlc)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), lct), TS_SUM(capx, 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When cash and earnings are exhausted, a firm's second line of defence is its trade assets: receivables can be factored and inventory liquidated, so non-cash working capital net of current claims measures the resources available to complete the capital program after the first line is gone.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic was right that `act` contains `che`, so this removes cash explicitly from the second leg, leaving trade assets net of current liabilities — a resource pool that is economically distinct from the cash and earnings in the first leg rather than overlapping with them. The claim being tested is a hierarchy of defences (earnings and cash first, liquidatable trade assets second), which is a different proposition from any single-tier coverage measure in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accounting Consistent Net Investment Surplus
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), DELTA(ppent, 1)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings are already net of depreciation, so subtracting gross capital spending double-counts the maintenance of the existing asset base; the funds genuinely consumed by expansion are the increase in net plant, and a firm whose earnings exceed that increment is self-funding its growth.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the one measurement flaw the critic identified twice and that I never addressed — the depreciation mismatch between `ib` and `capx`, which mechanically penalises utilities, transports and other high-depreciation industries regardless of their true funding position. The change is economic rather than cosmetic because it reclassifies every capital-intensive firm that is merely replacing worn-out plant from "strained investor" to "self-funding", and it needs only full-coverage balance-sheet items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Quick Asset Coverage Conjunction
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), ADD(lct, capx))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The liquid resources that can actually meet near-term claims and fund a capital program are cash and receivables; inventory is slow, discounted when sold under pressure, and often the very thing accumulating when a business deteriorates, so it should be excluded from the buffer.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has now bracketed this question — cash alone delivered α 5.0% while total non-cash working capital delivered only 3.1% — but the intermediate and economically correct measure, quick assets, has never been tested, and receivables are a large near-cash resource that the cash-only leg discards entirely. Excluding inventory also removes the one current-asset component whose growth is a documented *warning* sign, so this leg should be cleaner as well as broader than either extreme.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Consistent Surplus With Quick Liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), DELTA(ppent, 1)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), ADD(lct, capx))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is resilient when its sustained earnings cover the net expansion of its asset base relative to obligations and its cash and receivables cover near-term claims plus the capital program — the two funding conditions stated with internally consistent accounting on both sides.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the synthesis candidate for the family: it applies the depreciation repair to the flow leg and the quick-asset repair to the stock leg simultaneously, so if each fix helps individually this should be the strongest member, and if it matches rather than beats them we learn the two corrections address the same underlying noise. Coverage remains near the family maximum because every input is a standard balance-sheet or income item.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Total Outlay Coverage On Both Legs
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), MA(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), 3)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, MA(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), 3)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment is the sum of what a firm builds and what it buys, so both the surplus test and the required-liquidity test must be measured against total investment outlay averaged over the program horizon rather than against a single year of organic capital expenditure.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes the internal inconsistency the critic identified: total outlay now appears in both legs, and averaging it over three years matches the horizon of the earnings average, so lumpy one-off acquisitions no longer collide with a smoothed numerator. The economic content is a redefinition of what "investing" means for the whole family — serial acquirers, who are precisely the aggressive expanders the theme targets, are currently scored as if they invested nothing beyond plant.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unfunded Program Financed By New Claims
evaluated.hypothesis: A capital program that exceeds sustainable earnings is only value-destroying when the firm actually raised new claims to close the gap; a firm with the same shortfall that instead ran down its own cash or scaled back has not transferred value to creditors, so the financing *action* rather than the shortfall level identifies the damaged population.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the mirror-image corner the critic rejected with a short-side mechanism that is not the reflection of any long-side signal: the second leg is the one-year increase in the liability ratio, a financing action that appears in no successful archive member and that is conceptually independent of the shortfall magnitude in the first leg. Retaining gross capex here is deliberate and consistent — the cash leaving the firm, not the accounting net investment, is what has to be financed — so the signal identifies firms whose expansion was paid for by expanding the claim stack.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity Sized To Peak Commitment
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), ADD(lct, TS_MAX(capx, 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital programs are lumpy, so the buffer a firm needs is set by its heaviest spending year rather than by an average: quick assets that comfortably cover near-term claims plus the largest annual outlay of the past five years mean the firm can absorb its own peak commitment without external funding.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the smoothing ablation whose coverage rationale the critic correctly showed to be wrong, and replaces it with an untested economic claim about the shape rather than the level of the investment program — a firm spending 5% of assets every year and one alternating between 1% and 12% require very different buffers, yet every liquidity denominator tested so far treats them identically. Using the five-year maximum makes the required-buffer benchmark firm-specific and forward-looking in the sense that matters for a financing freeze, and all inputs remain full-coverage annual items.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt-Financed Capacity Buildout
considered.hypothesis: Physical capacity expansion is a bearish signal only when it is simultaneously accompanied by a rising debt ratio, because the marginal project is then financed by new fixed claims that raise default risk instead of by internally generated funds.
considered.reasoning: DELTA of the debt-to-assets ratio captures a genuine increase in balance-sheet fragility rather than mechanical growth in debt levels, while gross PP&E growth captures irreversible, hard-to-reverse investment. Their rank product is high only for firms leveraging up to build capacity, a combination historically followed by write-downs, covenant pressure, and weak equity returns.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Expansion Under Refinancing Pressure
considered.hypothesis: Capacity expansion is not uniformly bad; it is bad when the firm's debt is short-dated, so that long-lived illiquid assets must be continuously refinanced at the short end. The same expansion by a firm with long-dated debt is a resilience signal, because the investment horizon is matched to the funding horizon.
considered.reasoning: The conditioner is debt maturity structure (short-term share of interest-bearing debt), not leverage level, so it is close to orthogonal to CMA and to the documented leverage/distress effect that the critic flagged. Because ZSCORE centers the conditioner at zero, the interaction flips sign across the fragility dimension: high-growth firms with short-dated debt load the short leg and equally high-growth firms with long-dated debt load the long leg, so the spread cannot be reproduced by any monotone re-weighting of asset growth alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Gambling For Resurrection Intensity
considered.hypothesis: Reinvestment relative to the installed capital base is value-destroying in proportion to how deep a firm's accumulated earnings deficit is, because equity holders of firms with large historical losses have convex payoffs and prefer risky expansion over debt repayment.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the hard INDICATOR with a winsorized, standardized retained-earnings-to-assets conditioner removes the degenerate zero mass and the reliance on a small negative-book-equity subsample: every firm now receives a continuous score and coverage matches capx and re availability. Centering at zero makes the interaction genuinely two-sided, so heavy investors with deep accumulated profits form the long leg and heavy investors with accumulated deficits form the short leg, while low-investment firms of either type sit near zero and do not drive the spread.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Financing Gap Amplified By Thin Working Capital
considered.hypothesis: An investment program that exceeds internally generated cash flow is only dangerous when the firm has no working-capital slack to bridge it; the same gap at a firm with ample net working capital is a normal, self-correcting funding cycle rather than a solvency event.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the additive SUMRANK the critic identified as inconsistent with the stated mechanism: the funding-gap rank is non-negative and is multiplied by a centered working-capital z-score, so firms with no gap score near zero regardless of their balance sheet and the spread is identified purely off how the gap is cushioned. That construction breaks the standalone net-external-financing and cash-holdings effects, since a large gap can now appear on either the long or the short side depending on the slack available to absorb it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Unsold Capacity Build Under Solvency Strain
considered.hypothesis: Investment that shows up as unsold inventory rather than revenue is evidence that demand has not validated the expansion, and such unvalidated working-capital investment is followed by fire-sale markdowns precisely in firms whose current assets barely cover their obligations.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the rank-difference of asset growth and profitability that FF5 spans through CMA and RMW; the investment channel is now a change in inventory days (a real-quantity, demand-validation measure that is not an asset-growth or ROA proxy) and the distress channel is the Altman-style working-capital-to-liabilities cushion in centered form. The multiplicative structure means firms with stable inventory turns score near zero whatever their solvency, so the long-short spread is driven by the joint event of inventory accumulation plus a thin solvency buffer rather than by either well-known factor.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Conjunctive Self-Funded Resilience
considered.hypothesis: Financial resilience requires investment to be simultaneously self-funded and backstopped by liquid reserves; a firm scores high only if its operating cash flow covers its capital spending and its cash covers near-term obligations, and such firms are undervalued relative to their low refinancing risk.
considered.reasoning: MIN of the two ranks enforces the logical AND that the critic correctly noted SUMRANK does not deliver: a cash-rich firm that outspends its cash flow, or a self-funding firm with no liquidity, is capped at the low leg, so neither channel alone can produce a high score. It is also not merely the inverse of low investment, because a capital-intensive firm whose operating cash flow exceeds its capex still ranks highly, which separates the signal from CMA and from the short-side proposals in this set.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Conjunctive Distressed Overinvestment
considered.hypothesis: Reinvestment intensity relative to the installed capital base destroys equity value specifically at firms carrying high net debt, where new assets collateralize existing creditors and expansion is a levered bet rather than value creation.
considered.reasoning: This is the deliberate short-side mirror of the archive's winning conjunctive structure: the MIN of two ranks is high only when a firm is simultaneously a heavy reinvestor and net-debt-laden, so neither the asset-growth anomaly nor the leverage effect alone can drive the extreme decile. Netting cash out of total liabilities separates true balance-sheet strain from firms that gross up both sides, which is what makes it more than a CMA re-weighting.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Forced Contraction Under Illiquidity
considered.hypothesis: For fragile firms the danger is not only overexpansion but forced contraction: shrinking the productive capital base while working capital is thin relative to total liabilities indicates asset sales made under creditor pressure at distressed prices, which predicts further equity value destruction.
considered.reasoning: This deliberately probes the opposite corner of the investment-distress plane from every other proposal, testing whether the interaction is monotone in investment or U-shaped — an answer that reshapes the entire search direction regardless of outcome. If both this and the overinvestment conjunction earn negative alphas, the correct future construction is a distress-conditioned distance-from-normal-investment measure rather than a signed investment level.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Chronic Funding Gap With Short-Debt Reliance
considered.hypothesis: A single year of investment above earnings is a normal lumpy-capex event, but a persistent three-year gap funded at the short end of the maturity curve is a structural dependence on rollover markets that is punished when credit conditions turn.
considered.reasoning: The new element is persistence — the three-year moving average removes lumpy one-off capex from the investment leg — combined with a rollover-risk conditioner (short-term debt relative to cash) that is distinct from leverage level and therefore not spanned by CMA or by the other proposals here. If the persistent version dominates the one-year gap signal from generation 0, chronic external dependence rather than transient financing need is the priced state.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Self-Funded Expansion Without Leverage
considered.hypothesis: The rare firms that step up capital renewal while simultaneously reducing their liability ratio are demonstrating that expansion is being paid for out of internally generated cash; this revealed funding capacity is a forward-looking resilience signal that neither the investment level nor the leverage level discloses.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the archive winner's structure entirely rather than substituting one input: both legs are now first differences, so the signal is orthogonal to the profitability level and to the asset-growth level that the critic identified inside (ib − capx)/at. Because rising capex normally coincides with rising leverage, the conjunction isolates a genuinely small and economically meaningful corner — accelerating investment funded without new claims — and the MIN guarantees that deleveraging alone (a distress-recovery signal) cannot carry the long leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity Added Without Utilization
considered.hypothesis: Investment is validated by throughput, not by spending: when a firm's sales per unit of installed fixed capital deteriorates, the capital base has grown ahead of demand, and this overhang becomes an equity value problem specifically for firms whose expansion is locked in by long-term debt that cannot be scaled back with utilization.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the acquisition channel — which the critic correctly flagged as the published post-merger drift anomaly plus a degenerate COALESCE tie mass — with a capacity-utilization channel that has no tied values and full coverage from sale, ppent, dltt and at. Falling fixed-asset turnover is a change in productive efficiency rather than an investment or profitability level, so it is not spanned by CMA or RMW, and the long-term-debt conditioner captures the irreversibility that turns idle capacity into distress.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Runway Depletion Funding Capex
considered.hypothesis: What predicts distress is not the level of cash but its trajectory relative to near-term obligations: a firm spending heavily on fixed assets while its cash-to-current-liabilities coverage is actively eroding is consuming its own runway, and each additional quarter of that trajectory raises the probability of a forced financing event.
considered.reasoning: This drops sstk and therefore drops any overlap with the net-share-issuance and external-financing anomalies the critic named, replacing them with a liquidity-trajectory channel built from a first difference in coverage, which is not a documented standalone factor. The conjunction is essential and asymmetric: heavy investors whose coverage is stable or improving score low, and firms depleting cash without investing (ordinary operating losses) also score low, so only the self-inflicted runway burn survives into the short leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt Overhang Underinvestment
considered.hypothesis: Myers' debt overhang predicts that levered firms forgo investment because the gains accrue to creditors; firms whose capital spending has collapsed far below its own five-year peak while long-term debt remains heavy are trapped in this state, and the resulting erosion of the productive asset base is priced too slowly.
considered.reasoning: Scaling capex by its own five-year maximum makes the investment leg a firm-specific distance-from-peak measure that is scale-free and orthogonal to the cross-sectional investment level that CMA spans, which is a mechanism no archive signal has tested. It also refines the one accepted risk-taking signal (Forced Contraction Under Illiquidity, alpha −3.8%) by replacing a one-year contraction with a persistent multi-year investment drought and replacing generic illiquidity with the specific claim that causes overhang.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Headcount Expansion Without Earnings Cover
considered.hypothesis: Labor is the least reversible and most cash-hungry form of investment, so headcount expansion by firms whose earnings barely cover their obligations commits the firm to a fixed cost structure it cannot service, and the subsequent restructuring is not anticipated by investors focused on capital spending.
considered.reasoning: Employment growth is a real-quantity investment measure that appears in no FF5 factor and in no archive signal, and unlike capex it cannot be funded by depreciation or reversed by simply pausing a project. Conditioning on earnings-to-total-liabilities rather than on leverage keeps the fragility leg tied to debt-service capacity, so the top corner is specifically firms hiring into a coverage problem.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Erratic Capital Budgeting Under Accumulated Deficit
considered.hypothesis: The instability of an investment program, not its level, reveals whether capital allocation is planned or opportunistic; firms whose capex intensity swings wildly while they carry an accumulated earnings deficit are allocating capital reactively to funding availability, and such firms face higher realized distress costs.
considered.reasoning: This tests a second-moment investment concept that no factor model and no archive signal spans — every prior proposal used levels, changes, or persistence of investment, never its volatility — and pairs it with retained earnings, the Altman input that measures cumulative rather than current fragility. If instability carries information beyond the level, it justifies a whole family of second-moment conditioners for later generations; if not, we can drop the dimension cheaply.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Validated Versus Unvalidated Expansion
considered.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(sale, at), 1)), RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1))), MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(sale, at), 1))), RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Expansion is priced correctly only when the market can see whether it is being absorbed by demand: capacity growth accompanied by rising asset turnover is validated investment and should earn a premium, while identical capacity growth accompanied by falling turnover is unabsorbed capacity heading for write-downs.
considered.reasoning: This keeps the two-sided repair for the null-FMB problem but abandons the net-debt and cash-coverage constructs the critic identified, so the spread cannot collapse into a leverage-liquidity tilt: both corners share the same investment leg and differ only in the sign of the turnover change, making the signal a pure sign-flipping conditional that is near zero for non-investors. It therefore cannot be reproduced by CMA, which sorts on the level of growth without regard to whether output followed, and it uses only high-coverage annual items rather than the oancf-restricted sample.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Intangible Expansion Against Tangible Collateral
considered.hypothesis: Creditors lend against liquidation value, so a firm shifting the composition of its asset base toward intangibles while its liabilities already tower over its tangible capital is eroding the collateral backing its debt, raising both the probability and the deadweight cost of default.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the accrual-versus-cash ablation with an untouched economic axis — the composition rather than the level of investment — where the fragility conditioner is liabilities per unit of pledgeable tangible capital rather than any profitability or cash measure, so it is not a q-theory or RMW-CMA restatement. The conjunction matters because intangible-heavy expansion is benign at firms with light liabilities and heavy liabilities are survivable when backed by hard assets; only the joint state destroys recovery value.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity Growth Financed By Current Liabilities
considered.hypothesis: Funding long-lived, irreversible plant with an expanding stock of current liabilities — trade credit, accruals, and short-dated bank lines — creates a maturity mismatch that must be rolled continuously, so the same capacity build is far more fragile when the financing appears at the short end of the balance sheet.
considered.reasoning: This drops the tax framing the critic reduced to investment-times-low-profitability and replaces it with a financing-structure mechanism containing no profitability leg at all, so it cannot be a noisy RMW proxy. It also repairs the generation-0 proposal that the validator rejected for lacking a distress-exclusive variable, and it is distinguishable from the archived short-debt signal because it conditions on the *change* in current-liability intensity rather than on a static cash-coverage ratio.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash Resources Versus Committed Uses
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is a coverage ratio: total available internal resources — this year's operating cash flow plus the cash stock — measured against the claims that must be met in cash over the next year, namely the capital spending program plus maturing short-term debt.
considered.reasoning: This expresses the winning mechanism as a single smooth coverage ratio rather than a conjunction of two ranks, which makes it monotone over the entire cross-section and should produce an FMB slope and a decile spread that finally measure the same object. It is a genuine investment-distress interaction because the investment program sits in the denominator alongside maturing debt — capex is treated as a mandatory claim on cash, which is precisely the economics of the theme — and it is not a coverage ratio published as a standalone anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Persistent Expansion Despite Chronic Losses
considered.hypothesis: Current-year losses are noisy, but the frequency of loss years over five years identifies firms with a structurally unviable business model; when such firms sustain three consecutive years of heavy capital spending relative to their installed base, they are compounding a failing franchise with irreversible outlays.
considered.reasoning: Every archived fragility conditioner has been a current-period balance-sheet or income ratio, whereas loss *frequency* is the chronicity measure that the distress-prediction literature finds dominates single-period ratios, and pairing it with cumulative rather than one-year investment tests whether persistence on both sides sharpens the interaction. The tied values in the loss-frequency leg are economically meaningful buckets rather than a degenerate zero mass, and the MIN ensures profitable serial investors and chronically unprofitable non-investors both stay out of the short leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Funded Versus Unfunded Investment Ramp
considered.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(che, lct))), MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
considered.hypothesis: An acceleration in capital spending is good news when the firm already holds the liquidity to pay for it and bad news when it does not, so the *same* investment ramp should predict opposite returns depending on the liquidity state — the core claim of the investment-distress theme stated as a sign flip rather than as a level effect.
considered.reasoning: Both terms share an identical investment leg and differ only in the direction of the liquidity conditioner, so the signal is mechanically zero for firms not changing their investment rate and cannot reduce to either a standalone investment sort or a standalone cash-holdings sort — it measures only the interaction. It uses no cash-flow-statement item, so it tests the funded-versus-unfunded story on roughly 60% more firm-months than the archive winner, telling us whether the oancf coverage cost is worth paying.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Smooth Funding Capacity Product
considered.hypothesis: Funding capacity for the investment program has two multiplicatively interacting dimensions — how many times over this year's operating cash flow covers this year's capital spending, and how much of the near-term obligation stack the cash stock can retire — and firms strong on both are the resilient investors the theme predicts.
considered.reasoning: The critic's algebra is correct that any symmetric difference of a conjunction and its complement collapses to the additive rank sum, so instead of a two-sided construction I change the operator geometry: the rank product is strictly increasing in both legs everywhere, whereas MIN has zero gradient in whichever leg is currently larger, which is the most plausible reason the archive's MIN slopes were flat while its decile spreads were significant.
